problem: Mapless DRL navigation methods tend to memorize trained targets and fail to reach unseen targets in the same environment, especially when using monocular RGB input, where depth must be inferred.
motivation: Map-based planners (D*, PRM) need a known environment map, whereas animals build internal representations from experience. A mapless planner using only RGB and odometry that generalizes to new targets would be cheap and practical for mobile robots.
key_idea: Use a stacked two-layer LSTM policy trained with PPO on RGB image features plus relative target position (with the last velocity and reward as extra input), so that the agent reasons out paths to unseen targets rather than only memorizing trained ones.
insight: The authors report that a single LSTM layer was never better than stacked LSTM, but give no ablation numbers. Holding out test targets and placing many training targets across free areas (env2) shrinks the train/test performance gap seen in env1. The recurrent memory appears to let the agent infer depth from consecutive frames and direction from the relative target position.
method: Input encoding: 64x48x3 RGB passes through three conv layers (32/64/64 channels) and a 32-d dense layer; the target is given as relative polar coordinates (distance, angle).
Stacked LSTM: first LSTM (256) takes image features and the target; second LSTM (256) takes that output plus the previous reward and velocity; followed by a 256 dense layer and a 2-d output.
Output: linear velocity in (0, 0.3) m/s via sigmoid and angular velocity in (-1, 1) rad/s via tanh, i.e. continuous control.

Training with PPO (clipped objective) with an update every N episodes; training targets are separate from held-out test targets, and training stops when the success rate on the last 100 test episodes exceeds the goal (60%).
Reward: collision penalty, arrival reward, and a distance-difference shaping term c(d_{t-1}-d_t) minus a time penalty.
Sim-to-real: weights trained in env2 initialize training in a real indoor environment.

setting.backbone: CNN + stacked LSTM (2x256) + FC, trained from scratch with PPO
setting.training_data: RL interaction in two self-built Gazebo-style simulated indoor environments (env1, env2); real robot fine-tuned for 3000 episodes over three weeks
setting.observation: monocular RGB (64x48) + relative target position (odometry), previous velocity and reward
setting.action_space: continuous linear and angular velocity (max 0.3 m/s, 1 rad/s)
setting.simulator: custom simulated indoor environments (env1, env2) released as a benchmark

numbers_note: Results are mainly given as training curves (Figures 4 and 5); only the final success rates are in the text. There are no baselines or ablation tables.
results: The stacked LSTM planner reaches 81% success on new targets in env1 and 69% in env2 (target 60%), and 51% in a real environment after 3 weeks of training. The paper reports no numerical comparison against baselines.
limitations: Generalization is limited to unseen targets in the same environment (the second level); it does not generalize to new environments.
No baseline or ablation comparisons; the claim that stacked LSTM beats single LSTM is unquantified.
Real-world success is only 51% and training is slow (3 weeks); the evaluation uses small custom environments.
